sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Incline Push Up is a beginner-friendly push up variation performed with hands elevated on a bench or sturdy surface.

By raising the hands above the feet, the angle reduces the percentage of bodyweight being pushed, making it easier than a standard push up.

This exercise is an excellent progression tool for those working toward full push ups, and it primarily targets the lower chest, shoulders, and triceps.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.content:
- Easier than standard push ups, making it ideal for beginners
- Reduces load on the wrists and shoulders compared to floor push ups
- Targets the lower portion of the pectoralis major
- Builds foundational pushing strength for progression to harder variations
- Requires minimal equipment — just a bench, step, or sturdy surface
- Can be adjusted by changing the height of the surface
- Great for warm-ups or high-rep endurance sets

sections.heading: Muscles Worked
sections.content:
Primary: Pectoralis Major (Lower Chest), Anterior Deltoids (Front Shoulders), Triceps

Secondary: Core (Rectus Abdominis, Obliques), Serratus Anterior, Upper Back Stabilisers

sections.heading: Starting Position
sections.content:
1. Place your hands on an elevated surface such as a bench, step, or sturdy box.
2. Position your hands slightly wider than shoulder-width apart.
3. Step your feet back so your body forms a straight line from head to heels.
4. Keep your feet together or hip-width apart for stability.
5. Engage your core and glutes to maintain a rigid torso.
6. Arms should be fully extended with a slight forward lean.

sections.heading: Execution
sections.content:
1. Lower your body by bending your elbows, keeping them at approximately a 45-degree angle to your torso.
2. Descend in a controlled manner until your chest nearly touches the bench.
3. Keep your core braced and body in a straight line throughout the descent.
4. Push yourself back up to the starting position by straightening your arms.
5. Fully extend your arms at the top without locking out aggressively.
6. Exhale as you push up, inhale as you lower down.
7. Repeat the movement for the desired number of reps.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Letting the hips sag or pike up, breaking the straight body line
- Using a surface that is not stable or secure
- Flaring elbows out to 90 degrees, placing excess stress on shoulders
- Not lowering deep enough — aim for chest near the surface
- Placing hands too close together or too far apart
- Rushing the movement without control
- Not engaging the core throughout the movement

sections.heading: Equipment Needed
sections.content:
- Bench, step, box, or any sturdy elevated surface
- The higher the surface, the easier the exercise
- Ensure the surface is stable and will not slide
- Optional: Exercise mat for foot grip

sections.heading: Choosing the Right Height
sections.content:
1. A higher surface (e.g., countertop or wall) makes the exercise easier.
2. A lower surface (e.g., a low step or bench) increases difficulty.
3. Start with a height that allows you to complete 8-12 reps with good form.
4. As you get stronger, progressively lower the surface height.
5. The goal is to eventually progress to floor push ups.

sections.heading: Body Setup
sections.content:
1. Hands: Slightly wider than shoulder-width on the elevated surface.
2. Feet: Together or hip-width apart, on the floor behind you.
3. Core: Engaged throughout — maintain a rigid torso.
4. Hips: In line with shoulders and ankles — no sagging or piking.
5. Head: Neutral position, gaze slightly ahead of your hands.
6. Shoulders: Pulled down and back, away from ears.
7. Elbows: Track at roughly 45 degrees to your body during descent.

sections.heading: Similar Exercises
sections.content:
- Standard Push Up: Full bodyweight version for increased difficulty
- Knee Push Up: Alternative modified push up with knees on the ground
- Wall Push Up: Easiest push up variation, standing against a wall
- Bench Press: Barbell or dumbbell pressing for similar muscle targeting
- Decline Push Up: Feet elevated for increased difficulty and upper chest focus

sections.heading: Push Up Progressions
sections.content:
Wall Push Up: Easiest — standing upright pushing against a wall
Incline Push Up: This exercise — hands on a raised surface
Knee Push Up: Knees on the ground as pivot point
Standard Push Up: Full bodyweight from toes
Decline Push Up: Feet elevated for increased difficulty
Weighted Push Up: Adding resistance for advanced strength

sections.heading: If You Have Limitations
sections.content:
Wrist Pain: Use a surface that allows a neutral grip, or use push up handles
Shoulder Issues: Use a higher surface to reduce load on the shoulders
Lower Back Pain: Focus on core engagement and maintaining a straight back
Beginner: Start with a higher surface and gradually lower it over time
Need More Challenge: Lower the surface height or progress to floor push ups
Balance Issues: Use a wider foot stance for more stability
